# Simulating genomic data

The exercises in this chapter will pick up from where we left of in the chapter
on building _slendr_ demographic models, and use this as a basis to learn how to
simulate genomic data from these models.








## Preparation

 **To make sure we're all on the same page, saving the following code in a new
 script `slendr_scheduling.R`.** You can see that it's basically the outcome of
 the exercises in the previous chapter on building demographic models with
 _slendr_.

```{r}
#| output: false
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2) %>%
  resize(N = 100, time = 1800) %>%
  resize(N = 2000, time = 1000)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```









## Exercise: Simulating genomic data

Once we have compiled a _slendr_ model, we can finally simulate data from it. By
default, a simulation from a _slendr_ model always produces a
[tree-sequence](https://tskit.dev/tutorials/what_is.html) object as a result.
We'll explore the tree-sequence concept in a bit more detail later---for now we
can treat it as a black box which "magically" stores genomic variation of a set
of individuals.

There are two simulation engines built into _slendr_ implemented by functions
`msprime()` and `slim()`. For traditional, non-spatial, neutral demographic
models, the `msprime()` engine is much more efficient, so we'll be using that
for the time being.

::: aside

**Note:** The alternative engine implemented by the `slim()` function plays an
important role for spatial simulations and for simulations of natural selection
--- these are the primary two reasons why it's included in _slendr_ in the first
place.

:::

As we discussed in the introduction, here's how you can use simulate a tree
sequence from a compiled _slendr_ `model`. You will be seeing this kind of
pattern over and over again, so it's worth keeping it in mind any time you will
be simulating data going forward.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
ts <- msprime(
  model,
  sequence_length = <length of the simulated genome [in bp]>,
  recombination_rate = <uniform recombination rate [in crossovers per bp per generation]>
)
```

---

**Simulate a tree sequence from your compiled `model` by adding the appropriate
`msprime()` command into the script `slendr_scheduling.R`, storing it in a
variable `ts`. Set the parameters `sequence_length = 1e6` and
`recombination_rate = 1e-8`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

This command simulates a _tskit_ tree sequence from a _slendr_ model. Again,
note that we don't have to write any _msprime_ or _tskit_ code to implement the
simulation because _slendr_ does all the work for us!

```{r}
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)
```

:::

---

**Now type out the `ts` object in the console --- what do you see? Try to relate
some of the information in the presented summary to our overview discussion of
tree sequences. For instance, what are the "nodes" and "edges"? What's the
difference between "samples" and "individuals"? How many "trees" does the tree
sequence have, and how many "mutations" are stored in it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Evaluating the `ts` variable in the R console should give you a summary of a
tree-sequence object with some lower-level technical details about the genomic
sequence which it encodes:

```{r}
ts
```

For instance, our tree sequence contains genomic information for

`{r}
ts$num_individuals`, each of them diploid. This makes for `{r} ts$num_samples`
samples in total, where a "sample" is a "node" in a tree sequence representing
one haplotype (i.e., one chromosome) of a simulated individual. All other
"nodes" (of which there are many, many more) represent ancestral haplotypes of
these recorded individuals for which we generally have only a part of their
genomic information---a sequence information which made it through recombination
to some of the recorded samples.

:::

::: aside

**Note:** Similarly to the symbol `model`, whenever we from now on refer to
`ts`, we will be talking about some simulated tree-sequence object stored in an
R variable `ts`.

:::










## Exercise: Referring to simulated individuals

If we are to use tree-sequence data for computation of population genomic
statistics, we need a way to refer to individuals and populations. For this
purpose, _slendr_ provides three important functions: `ts_recorded()`,
`ts_names()`, and (sometimes, but not often, also useful) `ts_nodes()`. At the
bare minimum, these functions accept the tree sequence `ts` as their first
argument (i.e., can be run such as `ts_recorded(ts)`).

---

**Try answering these questions by running these three functions and inspecting
and comparing their outputs:**

- How many individuals are in your tree sequence based on these functions?

- How is the result of `ts_nodes()` different from `ts_recorded()`?

- What are the `time` values of recorded individuals based on the information
produced by these two functions? Are the `time` values the same in both?

- How many individuals in total are in the tree sequence based on these two
functions, and how many of them are in each population? Why do you get the
numbers you got, given the model which you programmed and simulated?

- How does `ts_names()` differ from the two table-producing functions?

**Hint:** Using table-manipulation functions of the _dplyr_ package might be
useful for this. Take a look at the chapter on manipulating tabular data using
_tidyverse_ packages, if you need a refresher.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

- The function `ts_recorded()` gives us a small metadata table with recorded
individuals' names, populations, and times:

```{r}
#| message: false
ts_recorded(ts)
ts_recorded(ts) %>% nrow()

library(dplyr)
ts_recorded(ts) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally
```

- The function `ts_nodes()` gives us a much larger table about tree-sequence
nodes, which includes not only information about recorded individuals
chromosomes (one node, or chromosome, for each individual), meaning that we get
two rows of the table for each individual:

```{r}
ts_nodes(ts)

ts_nodes(ts) %>% filter(name == "p1_42")
```

Additionally, the table also contains information about the recorded
individuals' ancestral haplotypes, i.e. individuals who lived in their
genealogical history, but whose complete genomic information we no longer have
(because they mostly likely passed only a subset of their genomes to the
individuals which we simulated or sequenced):

```{r}
ts_nodes(ts) %>% filter(time > 0)
```

**TODO:**

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

cowplot::plot_grid(ts_nodes(ts) %>%
  filter(is.na(name)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(time)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
    scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~is.na(name), scales = "free_x"),
  plot_model(model))
```

:::

## Exercise: Customizing sample recording

We can see that our tree sequence contains a massive number of individuals. Too
many, in fact --- we recorded every single individual alive at the end of our
simulation, which is something we're unlikely to be ever lucky enough to have,
regardless of which species we study.

To get closer to the scale of the genomic data that we usually work with, we can
restrict our simulation to only record a subset of individuals---we do this
using a process called "scheduling of recorded individuals" implemented by the
_slendr_ function `schedule_recording()`. Simply speaking, this is a
functionality of _slendr_ which precisely defines which individuals will be
recorded in the tree sequence while ignoring everyone else.

The function follows the structure in the following snippet, representing
another very useful pattern worth keeping in mind going forward:

```{r}
#| eval: false
schedule <- schedule_recording(
  <compiled slendr model>,
  times = <times of recording>,
  list(<population object>, <number of samples to record>),
  [... etc. ... ]
)
```

We then use this `schedule` object in a standard `msprime()` function call,
setting it as the argument of the same name (`schedule =`) like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

---

**To get an idea about what this function does in practice, modify the command
which simulates the `ts` object in your script `slendr_scheduling.R` according
to the snippet above, but include a schedule for recording 5 individuals from
each of the four populations. When you re-run the new simulation to get a new
`ts` object and type `ts` into your console, do you see a change? Again, use
your knowledge of `ts_recorded()` and some _dplyr_ table processing function to
inspect the recorded individuals.**

**Hint:** To make this easier to see, maybe keep the original simulation command
in your script (the one without the `schedule`) but modify it to create a
variable `ts_big` instead before you create the new `ts` object.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}
schedule <- schedule_recording(
  model,
  times = 0,
  list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 5), list(p4, 5)
)

# original simulation command (note the missing schedule)
ts_big <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

# new (smaller) tree-sequence recording
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)

# see that the new tree sequence is much smaller (even its memory footprint)
ts
ts_big

ts_recorded(ts)
ts_recorded(ts_big)

ts_recorded(ts) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally()
ts_recorded(ts_big) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally()
```

:::

::: aside

**Note:** In order to make recording of smaller number of individuals from a
(potentially huge) number of population easier, `schedule_recording()` supports
a shortcut of `list("all", <number>)` which records the given number of
individuals from every population in the model at the given time.

:::











## Exercise: Complex recording schedules

What if we need to simulate different number of individuals from different
populations at very specific times? Doing this with a single call to
`schedule_recording()` is not possible. Luckily, multiple schedules can be
easily combined together into a single sampling schedule.

---

**Type the `schedule` variable in your R console. What do you see? Why did I say
that multiple schedules can be easily combined? And how could we combine them?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

The output of any `schedule_recording()` function is a plain old data frame! It
contains a bunch of information we used in the `schedule_recording()` call
(population names, times, etc.), plus a bunch more additional data which is
currently irrelevant. For instance, notice the `time`, `pop`, and `n` columns
below:

```{r}
schedule
```

:::

Normally we don't ever have to look at this data (unless something goes wrong
with the sampling and troubleshooting _slendr_ itself is needed), but knowing
the format of the schedule means we can easily combine multiple schedules using
standard functions such as `rbind()` (included in base R).

---

In the following chapters, we will be working on implementing many real-world
scenarios from widely established research in population genomics, particularly
those from the field ancient DNA field. Naturally, in cases like this, we need
to be able to simulate sequences of "ancient" individuals as well as various
"present-day" reference panels.

In preparation for these complex exercises, **implement the recording schedule
summarized into the table below. You will have to figure out how many individual
schedules you'll have to create using `schedule_recording()`, then bind them
together using the function `rbind()` mentioned above. Then, simulate a tree
sequence `ts` with this new complex schedule, modifying your current solution
script accordingly.**

| time (years B.P.) | population | samples at each time | interpretation
|-------------------|:-----------|--------------|----------------|
| 0                 | p1         | 1            | outgroup |
| 0                 | p2         | 1            | admixture source |
| from 5 k B.P., every 1 k years | p3       | 5            | time-series of ancient individuals |
| 0                 | p4         | 10           | panel of reference individuals |

**Hint:** You can provide a vector of numbers as the `times =` argument of
`schedule_recording()`. See the help page for `?schedule_recording` for more
information and to see a concrete example.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Inspecting the table above, it looks like we have effectively two groups of
recording events determined by the times indicated in the first column: one
group of individuals in the "present-day" (i.e., at time 0) and a time-series of
ancient individuals. So let's leverage that to create two recording schedules,
"modern" and "ancient":

Scheduling of modern individuals:

```{r}
modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p2, 1), list(p4, 10))
modern
```

Scheduling of ancient individuals:

```{r}
ancient_times <- seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000)
ancient_times

ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = ancient_times, list(p3, 5))
```

We can then create a single sampling schedulie like this:

```{r}
schedule <- rbind(modern, ancient)
```

And use it in our simulation just like we showed above:

```{r}
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

Let's verify that we got the correct number of individuals:

```{r}
ts_recorded(ts) %>% group_by(pop, time) %>% tally
```

:::












## Exercise: Recording of named individuals

Sometimes, we don't just want to record a given set of "anonymous" individuals,
but we want to be able to work with unique, named individuals. This can be
especially helpful when we want to reconstruct a particular scenario in some
specific archaeological context (for instance, we want to work with some very
precious archaeological sample, such as the "Altai Neanderthal").

We can do so by calling `schedule_recording()` in a slightly modified way which
doesn't use the normal syntax `list(<population>, <number>)`, to record a given
number of individuals from the given population, but instead uses the format of
`list(<population>, 1, "<name of the individual>")`.

---

**Use this format to modify your recording schedule (for instance, based on
combining two recording schedules called `modern` and `ancient`) to implement a
unique recording event which will give the one representative individual of the
admixture source population the name `"source_ind"` and the outgroup individual
will be named `"outgroup_ind"`. Then create a new combined `schedule` again, and
verify that you got the newly named individuals in a new simulated tree sequence
`ts`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

We'll be more succinct now (see the full explanation to the `modern` and
`ancient` schedules in the solution to the previous exercise):

```{r}
outgroup <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1, "outgroup_ind"))
source<- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p2, 1, "source_ind"))
modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p4, 10))
ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000), list(p3, 5))

schedule <- rbind(outgroup, source, modern, ancient)
```

Now we can simulate a new tree sequence with more specifically named
individuals:

```{r}
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

And verify that we did everything correctly by inspecting the table of the
contents of the tree sequence:

```{r}
ts_recorded(ts) %>% print(n = Inf)
```

:::

---

**You may have noticed that `plot_model()` has a number of optional arguments.
One of them is called `schedule` and it accepts a sampling schedule (such as the
one you just created) as its input. Use your `model` and sampling `schedule` to
visualize your model.**

This functionality can be useful as an additional validation of your modeling
scripts, so always remember to use this for sanity checking your simulations
(after all, a picture can be worth more than <strike>thousand words</strike>
dozens of lines of code)!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's is the model on its own:

```{r}
plot_model(model)
```

Here is the model with sampling numbers overlaid on top:

```{r}
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)
```

:::

::: aside

**Note:** As you've seen above, the visualization is often a bit wonky and
convoluted with overlapping elements, so don't be too frustrated if the results
of your `plot_model()` visualizations are not too pretty. The function has been
designed as a validation and troubleshooting tool, rather than a tool to create
publication-ready figures.

:::

## Catch up

If you want to just catch up to the point at which this section would conclude,
here is the version of our simulation script at the end of the final exercise:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| collapse: true
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 10000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 2000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 5000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 2000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

outgroup <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1, "outgroup_ind"))
source<- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p2, 1, "source_ind"))
modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p4, 10))
ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000), list(p3, 5))

schedule <- rbind(outgroup, source, modern, ancient)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

:::
